utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Visnjic, do you have, either yourself or through Mr. Sepenuk, further submissions to make?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sepenuk -- [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]. On the question of the admissibility of this -- I'll call it report for the time being, and that's Prosecution Exhibit 473, I take it that's what Your Honour wants argument on. I will analyse -- we attempt to analyse this question based on the order on procedure and evidence that the Chamber issued yesterday. Needless to say, I'll be guided by that in my comments. And there are three relevant areas of that order that I think we should consider. First the admissibility or not of hearsay evidence; secondly, the admissibility of -- and I'll call it for the moment a book; and third, the admissibility of a report, because your order is directed to those three areas. And I'd like to start first, before I get into the hearsay matters, I'd like to start first with the book part of your order. And as the order states in general, books and other similarly lengthy documents, which of course this is of some 400 pages, will not be admitted in evidence in their entirety, but only parts will be admitted by the Trial Chamber if you consider it appropriate to admit it in light of the submission of the parties. In this case, as I understand it, the OTP is not making any kind of a claim as to part of the book. I've seen no submission by them that they want parts of this report admitted into evidence. They want the whole report admitted into evidence. Of course we'll hear from the OTP on this, but I'm assuming right now that they want the entire report in evidence for reasons I'll get to in a moment. I think that's unacceptable. The second part covered in the recent order are reports. And the Prosecution 473 is called an analysis of the human rights finding of the OSCE Kosovo Verification Mission. But certainly, for the sake of argument, we can call it a report. But obviously we don't have the situation of a report here because Your Honour's comments on reports are really directed to expert witnesses. And it's traditional that all or part of an expert witness report might be admissible. But we don't have that here. Ms. Mitchell was not called as an expert witness, nor does she qualify as an expert witness. Now, the report, of course, is classic hearsay, based, as it is, on unsworn, anonymous statements not subject to cross-examination. But I know that in the Tribunal that's not the end of the matter; it might be in some jurisdictions but it's certainly not the end of the matter, as we all know, in the Tribunal. And under Rule 89(C) in the cases of interpreting it, we have to determine whether despite the -- its hearsay nature, this document is reliable. As Your Honours have said in your recent order in paragraph 4: "The Trial Chamber considers that reliability of a hearsay statement is a necessary prerequisite for probative value under 89(C)." Now, what does the evidence under this point show about reliability? First, as the Trial Chamber noted yesterday, we have to look to the teachings of the Appeals Chamber in the Aleksovski case, quoted again in your order. We have to look as the Appeals Chamber noted in that case - and I'm going to quote now - to "the infinitely variable circumstances which surround hearsay evidence." And the first thing we should look at, I respectfully suggest, is the report itself; OTP Exhibit 473. So we open this document, and the first thing that greets us on page 6 - as I understand in the scanned materials it's little 5 in the booklet I have - is the acknowledgment by Ambassador Gerard Staudmann who is the director of the OSCE and he says after noting the generous --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just hold a second. I happen to have a copy of this but other Judges don't because it's not available in hard copy but it's on here. So let's have that page on --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- the e-court. You say it's page 5 in e-court, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes, it's page 6, as I understand it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, it's page 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: On OTP Exhibit 473.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, I have it on the computer screen but not on the -- yeah, we have it now on both.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. As noted in that acknowledgment after first -- after Ambassador Staudmann first notes the generous financial support of certain western European countries and the United States in making possible the report, it goes and says: "The OSCE ODIHR is grateful for the advice and assistance of staff of the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, ICTY, in the development of this report." And of course as we know from the evidence that we've heard, the ICTY and the OSCE were in daily contact in assembling information for this report, and the OTP, I think it's fair to say, took a very significant part in the assembling of information and in the writing of this report. If we turn to page 7 of the report, if that could be put up on the screen. Next page, yes, the foreword. And of course that's the foreword from Justice Louise Arbour who, as we all know now, was the lead Prosecutor of the Tribunal during this period in 1999. She said a number of complimentary things in this foreword. And she, of course, is the Prosecutor who signed the indictment in this case in 1999 when it was initially brought against three of the defendants in this case. So even though the OSCE was not technically employed by the OTP, as a practical matter it was the OTP's chief investigator in this case. This report, OTP Exhibit 473, provided the blueprint for the OTP in this case. If this report is considered admissible by the Trial Chamber, you might as well admit the Prosecution's pre-trial submission in this case, you might as well admit Mr. Hannis's opening statement in this case, you might as well admit the government's closing argument in this case. That analogy, I respectfully suggest, is apt and suitable. This report should not be admitted into evidence. This report is a series of allegations not based on reliable evidence or proof. Finally, in determining the reliability of the report we ask the Trial Chamber to consider the testimony of Sandra Mitchell. Now, what was the importance of her testimony? I would like to read very briefly from the OTP's summary of what -- of what they regard as the importance of Ms. Mitchell's testimony. This was simply a summary they furnished in the case about Ms. Mitchell. And they said, OTP said: "All information used in the preparation of 'As Seen, As Told' was collected and managed under the direct supervision of the witness. At all times she had primary responsibility for ensuring the credibility of the human rights findings made and the integrity of the conclusions drawn." Now, what do we know about Ms. Mitchell? What have we learned about her in this courtroom? We know that to this day she is deeply engaged in the welfare of the Kosovo Albanians. She is to this day the head of the United Nations mission for return of refugees to Kosovo. Second, she was the OSCE "primary liaison" with the OTP, dealing with that office on virtually a daily basis of supplying information to them regularly and repeatedly. Three, she had as she conceded a very "special relationship" with the Albanian population from Kosovo; again, a relationship which continues to this day. Now, let me digress for a second here. I'm not deprecating Ms. Mitchell. I take my hat off to anybody involved in humanitarian work. They do marvelous work, and again I respect them. But those qualities of passion and commitment that go into that work sometimes will create -- at least it's my experience, and again the collective experience of this Chamber is far greater than mine, but I will simply note something that I think is a matter of common sense, those qualities of passion and commitment that go into this kind of work sometimes create: We're the only good guys in the room philosophy. We're the good guys and the other people are the bad guys. And I suggest that those kind of qualities are not quite the qualities one wants for detached dispassionate analysis, for objectivity, for reliability. Now, I think hat it's clear that Ms. Mitchell show these -- this lack -- and again I'm saying it with respect for her. I don't mean to unduly deprecate her. But I think that she showed a certain lack of objectivity in a number of ways in her testimony. I'll simply cite a few. Her grudging concession that the NATO bombing might have been responsible for the departure of the KVM on March 20, 1999. It took a series of questions for her finally to make that concession. Secondly, the question of thousands of interviews, she originally stated in Milosevic trial and in her statements about thousands of interviews and she gradually paired that down. At one point she said a little less than 10.000. And then finally she came up with a 3300, 4300 figure. And I mentioning that -- and I want to mention that, too, in connection with -- not to beat this point to death either, but Mr. Stamp saying tens of thousands of interviews. That alone at least is giving the Defence a lot of concern here, but where are these -- to this day we haven't received a single refugee verification form in the form noted when she testified yesterday. I think it was Prosecution Exhibit 765. We've had reports about that form. We've yet to see one of those forms and we've yet to be given any intimation about all these thousands of interviews and what happened there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Perhaps I misunderstood Mr. Visnjic yesterday, but he was saying that you had received a very small number of these forms.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: No, we actually have not received the forms themselves, Your Honour. Remember the refugee verification form, it says: Reasons for leaving and that kind of thing, and it was made out in handwriting. We have not received a single one of these forms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: None of these -- so all you have received --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Is a typewritten report about what, presumably, was in that form. And finally I want to -- I am asking the Chamber to recall - and I know you do recall - Ms. Mitchell's testimony about the word-for-word duplication of the International Crisis Group report and the OSCE report. And if I could just quote briefly from her testimony. And I asked her after showing her two instances in which the ICG report was exactly the same as the OSCE report, I want to represent to the Court that my colleague, Mr. Visnjic -- I make this representation to the Court. My colleague, Mr. Visnjic, has now found three more reports which are literally word for word the same. And I asked her: "So is the only conclusion that we can draw from this is that somehow the ICG was privy to your information?" She says: "No, as I've stated we had the measures in place to ensure as best we could the security and the confidentiality of the information. There were a lot of people following and getting statements. People were working together. The rule was, you know, the information was only being shared with ICTY. And if, you know, somebody breaks the rule, they break the rule. But that's as much as I can say on it, Your Honour. "Q. So what you're saying here is that at least based on what you're saying it appears that one of your investigators shared information with the International Crisis Group against the rules of your organisation. "A. It's a possibility. It's also that possibility that this person re-interviewed somebody hat we had interviewed and came up with the same story." I said: "Word for word?" Ms. Mitchell said: "Sure." I then said: "That's your testimony?" She said: "Anything's possible. I have given, you know, the reasons that I can think of as honestly as I can, and if they shared a form, they shared a form, and, yeah, the rule was broken." I found that testimony very, very disturbing. Here's the person charged with ensuring the credibility of this report, and she actually testified under oath that, yes, in this terribly chaotic situation with all these Albanian interviews in this horrible refugee camp situation that, in at least two instances, and I'll be charitable now and I'll confine it to just this one instance, she said it's possible that word for word it still could have been a different interview. That defies credibility. And if that's her notion of credibility, I think is this report should be considered very -- to be a very dubious document if she is the person in charge of ensuring the credibility of the report. I think at the very least it casts very severe -- it casts very serious doubt on her judgement. And again, let's assume also, let's assume that a rule was broken, a rule was broken. How many other rules were broken? I mean, was there was a trafficking -- and I don't mean this frivolously, because again I admire deeply the work these people were doing. But based on her testimony it seems like there was almost some sort of trafficking in these refugee forms. People were following along. One organisation was following another organisation, and if one or more members of her organisation broke the rules, what other rules did they break? Did they break the rules on objectivity, on credibility, on being fair, on being dispassionate? And I ask Your Honours to consider that, and we ask Your Honours to reject this report. We respectfully submit that receiving this report into evidence would be a mistake, it would be unfair, it would be unjust.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sepenuk. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm going to ask you to not admit Prosecution P473, As Seen, As Told, and I have two basic submissions. And they are first that this is inadmissible hearsay; and second, that as a result of breaches in the rules of disclosure on the part of the Prosecution they should be barred from presenting this exhibit. I will not repeat what Mr. Sepenuk has said; I will adopt it. What I would like to direct the Chamber to one further Appeals Chamber decision, which we say may be helpful in the resolution of this issue, and that's from the Kordic case, IT-95-14/2 AR 73.5, a decision of the Appeals Chamber of 21 July 2000, where the Appeals Chamber stated that Rule 89(C) must be interpreted so that safeguards are provided to ensure that the Chamber can be satisfied that the evidence is reliable. The point being that there's a threshold question which the Appeals Chamber spelled out at paragraph 22 of that decision. It's the following: "The reliability of the hearsay statement is therefore relevant to its admissibility and not just to its weight." We say that the lack of reliability, given the full context of the way in which these hearsay statements were used, does not satisfy the threshold question of admissibility. What do we have? The report contains an assessment of the statements of others, which we say is based on unreliable and biased methods of data collection. There can be no probative value to hearsay taken in that regard. Your Honour, we take issue with the qualifications, competence, and bias of the persons who took this information which is -- forms the basis of this document. We've heard and we can see, as a matter of common sense, that there was selective sampling. There's indications that there may have been a manipulation in the selection of individuals who came forward, chosen by community leaders, who one would have to think were sympathetic to the cause of the KLA. Ms. Mitchell has acknowledged that there was a lack of training of people performing the task; they received on-the-job training, as she put it. And she acknowledged that their training was not followed up and, at best, was haphazard and sporadic. Your Honour, we say that against Rule 89(C) you must consider Rule 95 of our Rules of Procedure and Evidence. It's a very short rule, and it states that: "No evidence shall be admissible if obtained by methods which cast substantial doubt on its reliability or if its admission as antithetical to, or would seriously damage, the integrity of the proceedings." I'll stop there on this first point that I wish to make, given that Mr. Sepenuk has canvassed it quite fully. The second point I wish to make in support of our request to not have this exhibit admit is what we say is a violation of Rule 68(ii) by the Prosecution. Now, I commend my learned friend from the Prosecution for informing us, quite candidly, that there was a large amount of material which was never -- has never been disclosed by the Prosecution to the Defence. I do take issue, however, with my learned friend from the Prosecution when he suggests that the obligation was on the Defence under Rule 66(B) to request that information. With all due respect to the Prosecution, Your Honour, we disagree. Rule 68(ii) places an affirmative obligation, a mandatory obligation on the Prosecution to make available to the Defence under the EDS system materials which it has at its disposal. We've heard from Ms. Mitchell that the Prosecution has had this material for years. Why do I say that Rule 66(B) does not apply? The Chamber will be aware of the legislative history of these rules and Rule 66(B) is the remnants of the old reciprocal disclosure rule. As you know, reciprocal disclosure is no longer part of our rules of procedure. Rule 66(B) does say that Defence can make a request for certain materials; it does say that. But the primary rule in regard to disclosure, the disclosure obligation by the Prosecution is Rule 68(ii). That's an affirmative obligation that the Prosecution must disclose to us under that provision using the electronic disclosure system. We say that there's been a breach of their disclosure obligation, and Rule 68 bis provides for a consequence for failure to comply with the disclosure obligation. Rule 68 bis says: "The Chamber made decide at the request of other party on sanctions to be imposed on a party which fails to perform its disclosure obligations pursuant to the Rules." We say that the only relief that would be meaningful now that we are in trial, now that we have learned that there has been a breach of their obligation under 66(ii), some seven years later, is that this report should not be admitted since the underlying material has not been made available to us. We say again Rule 95 comes into play, and it would put these -- it would bring these trial proceedings into disrepute to do otherwise. So on either score, whether it's the inadmissible hearsay or the violation of Rule 68(ii), in conjunction with the jurisprudence of the court and Rule 95, we respectfully submit that you should rule in our favour and not admit this Prosecution Exhibit P473 into evidence. Those are my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. O'Sullivan. Can I deal just now with what might seem a very petty point but it actually has a purpose in due course. These divisions of Rule 68 are Roman numeral divisions. I know there are questions of alphabet and approach to letters between the two languages and it's easily understood what you're referring to here, Mr. O'Sullivan, but a difficulty can arise in relation to the indictment because the letter I appears in subparagraphs of the indictment, and you can end up with an I -- I don't know if it actually happens in this indictment, but I and then subparagraph, as you would describe it, (ii) or (iii). So I think we should adopt a routine approach to this and use -- it regard these as Roman numerals, and you'll see the same feature in the indictment itself. Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will not reiterate the words of my colleagues, since our position is to adopt everything put forth by our colleagues. We intended to mention several things, but due to the lack of time we will try to narrow that to the very basic objections we have as regards this document. I wanted to draw your attention to several decisions of this Tribunal which may be relevant, in my view, in your -- for your deliberations. In the Tadic case, decision -- motion on hearsay dated the 5th of August, 1996, inter alia, it states that the Rules of Procedure and Evidence implicitly require that the reliability be one of the components of admissibility. In that decision, one also reads that in order for the Trial Chamber to be able to examine the circumstances, it is necessary to assess the reliability of every given piece of evidence and draw conclusions based on that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, we haven't received the text of the decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another decision dated the 19th of January, 1998, it states that reliability is an implicit component of admissibility of evidence in case it is clear that any submitted exhibit is clearly unreliable cannot be considered of any probative value. Based on everything stipulated by my colleagues and based on the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, in our view, and according to Rule 98(D) -- 99(D) --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 89(D) shows -- or rather, mentions the actual points I've made previously as regards the admissibility of this report. In our view, it should not be admitted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, the name of the case on the 19th of January, 1998?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Prosecutor versus Delalic and others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Aleksic, do you have any submissions to make on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not as regards this. But I was told by my lead counsel to read out a text of our objections, should I be permitted to do so. And I believe this would be a favourable time before we move on to the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is an objection to what?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, regarding the right to counsel of General Pavkovic. And, with your leave, I'd like to state a couple of points that we would like to have in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is not an appropriate time for you to be making a general point in relation to the conduct of the trial. If you have a submission to make, then you should make it in writing. If you have a particular submission to make on the question of the admissibility of this evidence, then I will hear you on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I simply follow the instructions of my lead counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I believe everything has been said and we second the things that have been said. What I wanted to add is that the document discussed here also contains some legal arguments or positions which are inadmissible, in our view, and they comprise a very important portion of the report itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. If I may briefly start by responding to some of the objections raised today. It is submitted that the OTP took a significant part in the assembly of the information, and that is a quote from one of the submissions. There is no evidence that the OTP participated in the collection of the information. There is evidence, and it is agreed, that when the analysis was being done there was advice and assistance from the ICTY and that the raw material, the refugee forms, were delivered to the ICTY and there was contact with the ICTY quite frequently. The mere fact that the then-Prosecutor of the ICTY wrote a congratulatory foreword to the report does not, in any way, detract from its reliability or its objectivity. The ICTY is a Tribunal set up by the United Nations for the prosecution of crimes of the nature charged in this indictment. The KVM mission in Kosovo was a mission acting under the auspices of a United Nations resolution, and it is normal, practical, indeed it is desirable, that there should be amicable relations, cooperation, and advice and assistance between the parties. And the fact that there was this type of relationship does not detract from the independence of the OSCE-KVM mission and does not in any way suggest that there was undue or improper interference from the ICTY. It was said in addition to that that the witness, Sandra Mitchell, may have been tainted by -- I'm not sure, maybe bias because of her ongoing work in human rights or humanitarian issues. It is suggested that she is presently engaged in the welfare of the Kosovar Albanians, and that's another quote from the submission. There is no evidence as to that. She is the director for the return of refugees, refugees. There were refugees of various ethnicities leaving Kosovo. Indeed she testified that she prepared a report in respect to offences that were committed against the Serbs in Kosovo after June of 1999, and the evidence in respect to the return -- her work as the director for the return of refugees is indicative of her work in respect of the return of Serb refugees. So it is not correct to say that she's engaged -- still engaged in the welfare of Kosovar Albanians. And in fact if she was still engaged, it is my submission that that would not sufficiently detract from her credibility so as to render the report inadmissible. The issue of Rule 95(F). It is submitted that Rule 95(F) is relevant to the issues in respect to the report. It is the Prosecution's submission that the Rule 99 -- 95, I beg your pardon, Rule 95, which is what I'm discussing, was primarily intended to ensure the integrity of the Tribunal's proceedings, rendering inadmissible evidence which was obtained through oppressive conduct. The method of obtaining the evidence is a critical issue when Rule 95 is being considered. For example, evidence which might be obtained on an involuntary basis. So a mere reference to Rule 95 in this context, it is my submission, does not suffice to invoke it insofar as we are talking about a report of this nature. And there is an issue in respect to disclosure. The issue of disclosure, as Your Honour well knows, is a complex thing, what is Rule 68 and what is within the knowledge of the OTP. The -- there are criticisms from the Defence on many occasions in this case about material being disclosed to them which is of marginal Rule 68 value and of them being flooded with material disclosed to them under Rule 68 which they find useless. I've heard many complaints about that. The approach -- one of the approaches that could be made in respect to huge databases of material is that once the Defence is made aware of what it is, then if they consider it to be Rule 68, or if they think that it is useful to the preparation of their Defence under Rule 66, then being so forewarned they ought responsibly to make a request for the information. As I indicated before, what we are speaking about is raw data, thousands of forms from various sources collected in the field, some processed and put on the EDS and therefore available to the Defence; and some not so. The witness who has been on the -- a previous witness list filed said in this statement which is now evidence -- in her statement, which is now evidence before the Court, that the material was delivered to the OTP; that is, the raw data. The raw data is generally, insofar as I -- as the results of my inquiries have revealed, not Rule 68. It is the opposite of Rule 68. The Defence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You seem to be suggesting that this is some lower category of material, raw data. I would have thought that raw data was exactly what the Court should be most interested in, the basic material, the source material.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The Court ought -- and of course the Defence ought to be most -- or at least generally interested in the source material. I refer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Remind me of why it is you say that the Defence ought to have been alerted to the existence of all these statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The exhibit itself, which has been on the exhibit list, indicates that the statements were -- were given -- the originals were given to the OTP in 1999. So the Defence would have been aware of it from that. But the statement of the witness, which has been served on the Defence many times over the years, the last few months, also says quite clearly that the material, which I refer to as raw data, was handed over to the OTP after they were photocopied. So I would submit that the Defence, in preparation for the trial, would have, if they thought it fit and thought it's something that the Court would want to look at, these thousands of forms, that would be useful to the deliberations, would have asked for them. They asked for those in respect to those persons who are going to testify. We have made efforts to give them those forms. We gave them the data reports -- I shouldn't say "the data reports," the print-outs from the database. We are now searching for the originals of those individual persons because they are among batches, huge batches, of material which we received some six years ago. It was yesterday that a general request for the first time was made for all the material, and we are now in the process of gathering together all the material. And it is a process that involves work and deployment of staff and effort. So the disclosure of this material is a matter which the Defence could have achieved, could have enforced, if they thought it relevant to the trial from long before we came into this court to proceed in the trial. And without being critical or anything, I would submit that it would not be the time now, in the course of a trial, to use this setting to criticise the Prosecution for non-disclosure of material of that nature. Indeed, I suspect that if all of this material had been disclosed, then we might have been criticised for inundating the Defence. I think -- I submit that it was sufficient that we gave them adequate notice that the material existed, and therefore if it was appropriate for them to use it in their preparations, they could have asked for it. And much has been said about hearsay. It is agreed and accepted that -- I think by all that hearsay is admissible in the Tribunal. And reliability, of course, is an important issue in respect to the admissibility of hearsay. I don't think we would need authority on that. There is a lot of evidence before the Court in respect to the reliability of the methods of collections, notwithstanding the criticisms which have been made by the Defence. The -- indeed, it is my submission that Your Honour may well consider the answers given by the witness in cross-examination yesterday, when counsel elicited material which are apparently consistent with the averments -- the averment of the Defence in respect to the facts in issue. The -- this material suggests that the witness in the discharge of her responsibility to gather the material and to write this report approached her work with objectivity. The evidence is that they took appropriate steps to train their staff in the collection of these reports; to employ, as far as possible in the circumstances - which must have been somewhat chaotic at the beginning - but to employ, as far as possible, persons with adequate experience. And after they had gathered the information, when they were forced -- not forced. When they were allowed to return to Kosovo, as the report indicates and as the witness said in testimony, they took steps, whatever steps possible, to verify the accuracy and the reliability of the information that they were using to formulate the report. As the report indicates, where there were inconsistencies they reported it; where there were weaknesses, they reported it. And the report, in that sense, speaks for itself. The report is, in fact, a well-documented analysis with appropriate citations of the victim reports, and that is very important. This is not second-hand hearsay; these are identifiable victims. And it was carried out under the mandate given to them by United Nations resolution. So the objections in respect to the evidence of the witness and her -- whether she's biased or not, whether she's -- she's pro-Albanian or anti-Serb are really objections which go to weight. They are objections, which it is submitted, refer to matters, if they are worthy, but they are matters which we could leave to the good judgement of this Chamber when considering the weight of the document. But it is submitted they are not matters that should be considered in the initial deliberations in respect to the admissibility of the documents. The Strugar case was referred to yesterday. This was a case in which a report which, according to the Defence, was of a similar nature to this one was rejected. It is the submission of the Prosecution that the report in Strugar is quite distinct from this one, and I will just give two other reasons, and there are other important reasons why it is really distinct. The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Who referred to Strugar, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think it was Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it was I who mentioned it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson is not here. I think I'm wrong there. The critical point in the Strugar decision in rejecting that report was that the date, the date of the incident that that report referred to could not be ascertained. Or if I could put it this way, the report referred to incidents that occurred between October and December. The issue in that case was an incident of one day in December, and it could not be clearly discerned whether or not a report which covered that broad period could be narrowed on the focus on that issue before the Court, the one being in December. The other distinction with that case is that the report in Strugar was a preliminary report, and I think that was the main reason why it was not accepted. It was titled a preliminary report to the extent that one of the consultants involved in preparing the report, when he came to testify in Strugar could not even vouch for the accuracy of that report. So that report in Strugar is clearly distinguishable from what we have here. The said same report, As Seen, As Told was received in evidence in the Milosevic case. And I'm not suggesting for a minute that because it was received in a previous case that you are bound by it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I would be assisted if someone could explain to me how it was received in the Milosevic case, and you may care to have a look at that. I've tried myself to work out on what basis it was admitted and it's far from clear. Although you're right, it was given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I was trying to work that out myself, and I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think it slipped in in circumstances where an accused was not adequately represented at that stage and perhaps not quite as switched on, as he later was, to the conduct of the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In that case, though, I think that the Court did go to distinguish As Seen, As Told from material which would not be acceptable in evidence because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I've been unable to find the decision admitting it. So if you could find it, I would be grateful if you were able to assist me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I will endeavour to find the decision admitting it. But it was referred to in the transcript by the Court at page 5643, in which the Court indicated -- and here I'm going off of a reference to it in an appeal judgement, in the same Milosevic case, a judgement -- decision on admissibility of Prosecution investigators' evidence, a judgement of the 30th of September, 2002. It was distinguished from a non-admissible document because it was not prepared for the purposes of that particular trial, and it had been prepared by a body independent of the parties, and thus has a quality of independence. As submitted before, the association, close association, amicable and cooperative relationship between the ICTY and the KVM-OSCE mission does not detract from the independence of the report, and neither was it prepared for this trial specifically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is your transcript reference to the trial transcript in Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The trial transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And then the appeal decision separate, or was that transcript -- is that a page in the transcript where the appeal decision was being discussed?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The appeal decision that I just referred to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- referred to the Milosevic decision on As Seen, As Told and cited that transcript number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It was also received evidence in the Limaj case, where the accused was represented, as Exhibit 150. And while I'm on the Limaj case, the report by Human Rights Watch under orders was also received in that case as evidence and, indeed, cited in the Judgement. As I say, I don't claim at all that the Court is bound by these decisions; I know that the Court is entitled to exercise its discretion on the basis of the facts before it in this case. And I submit that the evidence from Ms. Mitchell not only indicates -- and we're not talking about beyond a reasonable doubt, but well beyond prime facie that proper efforts were made to induct appropriate staff, to train them where necessary, and to collect the information on an objective and reliable basis. So there are sufficient indicia of reliability for the report to be admitted. Unlike a previous report, this is not a report based on double hearsay; this is a report based on identifiable victims, the actual victims. The Court is entitled, within the exercise of its good judgement, to use the whole report - and here I refer to the objection based on the submission that the whole report should not go in - to use the whole report in its deliberations. I pause here to ask the Court to consider the objections in respect to the opinions expressed in the report in respect to law. There are many areas of the report where the law is discussed. Now, clearly if any party to these proceedings should submit to the Court that you should take the law as discussed in As Seen, As Told, then the Court, in the exercise of its good judgement, could deal with that appropriately. However, the discussion of the law in the report is relevant to the context in which the persons who did the analysis conducted their job. The whole of the report provides the context in which the various parts, the various areas of the analysis, was done. And the Prosecution has faith in the judgement of the Tribunal, of the Trial Chamber, should inappropriate submissions be made at a later date as to how the various areas of the submission -- of the report should be used. The Prosecution does not proffer the report or tender the report as direct evidence in proof of any of the specific incidents or crime sites referred to in the indictment, but submits that if -- or will submit at the appropriate time that if, as we anticipate, direct evidence which we will call establishes to the satisfaction of the Trial Chamber that these offences were, in fact, committed, then the report can assist the Trial Chamber and give it whatever weight the Trial Chamber thinks appropriate. In corroborating the evidence the evidence in respect of these crime scenes, it can assist the Trial Chamber in its deliberations on the issue of the widespread and systematic nature of the offences charged. It can assist the Trial Chamber on the issue of notice to the higher level political and military figures of crimes committed, not only in 1998 but also in 1999. And it can assist the Trial Chamber in respect to its analysis of evidence relating to the background of the conflict and the parties involved in the conflict. In all of these areas, the degree to which it is of assistance is squarely, it is my respectful submission, a matter of judgement for the Trial Chamber. But the whole document is admissible, may it please Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, I have a number of matters to raise with you. First of all, do you wish to address the point made by Mr. Ivetic about Rule 92 bis?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The submission in respect to Rule 92 bis is that the Prosecution at this stage does not submit the evidence of these 2.800 persons in evidence. The statements are the basis of the report. If we had sought to put in directly the evidence of any one of them, we would have either to call the witness here or ask for it to be received under Rule 92 bis. The witness called was Sandra Mitchell, and the issue really, I think, which Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I must have misunderstood because I thought 12 of them were to give evidence? Have I got that wrong?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: 12 will give evidence. But you won't be submitting their statements?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Some of them, I believe. We applied for them to be received under 92 bis. Some were live. All of them will come to testify, having regard to the recent ruling of the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ivetic's point is that that's just a way around Rule 92 bis, which says that where you're relying on a statement, then there are certain requirements, and these aren't followed in this case. And you get around them by saying somebody else will report on what that witness has said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The -- it is submitted that Rule 92 bis - and I hope I'm not being repetitive - applies to the direct evidence of the witness, if the witness's testimony is being placed before the Court, or if an attempt is made to place the witness's testimony before the Court. Here we have an analysis of the statements of witnesses who are not called to testify and it is submitted that the appropriate consideration is really whether or not the hearsay has sufficient indicia of reliability for limited purposes. For example, if the Court accepts the other evidence we lead in respect to the several crime bases, the Court will have to at some point deliberate upon matters of widespread, systematic nature in which the offences were committed. While the report, it would not be our submission, could stand or prove by itself something of that nature. The Court may, it is my submission, refer to the various statements used in the report and give it whatever weight it thinks fit. But it is a vexed issue. How many witnesses does one call to prove widespread and systematic? Certainly not the 800.000 that we allege left Kosovo. We call a fraction of that. But could a report which covers a large amount of those persons assist the Court in its deliberation? And it is the Prosecution's submission that in that area, for example, the report is of legitimate use.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, in the -- in the report there is an index and there are 30 municipalities in the index.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: 30. And there are 13 in the case. What's the Trial Chamber to do with the ones which are not referred to in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In respect to the ones not referred to in the indictment, the report itself could not provide any collaboration of any evidence led because we will not be leading evidence in respect to those. However, the indictment does charge for all of Kosovo. The specific -- incidents specified in the indictment are a representative sampling. Indeed the Chamber did reduce them. It is impractical for us to prove or attempt to prove all of them. But at some point the Court will have to consider the core allegation of the indictment, that this was a Kosovo-wide endeavour, not limited to the illustrative sampling that is represented or identified in the indictment. So the report, it is submitted, can be used by the Trial Chamber in its deliberations under evidence in respect to the specific crime bases or crime sites charged and in respect to the report's discussion of areas which are not within the indictment. It can assist the Trial Chamber in its deliberation on the bigger picture, the Kosovo widespread, systematic offences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, can you remind me how that's presented in the indictment so I see how it would match with the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Without referring to specific passages in the indictment, the indictment, in my submission, refers to the averment in the indictment, that the offences were not limited to those charged specifically in the indictment but were widespread and systematic and were persecutory of the general Kosovar Albanian population in Kosovo. I think that averment is made at various places in the indictment, which I don't have with me now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Certainly it's something I've overlooked. So far I thought this was an indictment about 13 municipalities, which was a basis for saying that this was widespread and systematic behaviour. I would be assisted by being shown where the indictment says that it extends beyond these areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm having a look at the electronic copy. I would be able to assist the Court in a moment. For example, it has been pointed out to me, paragraph 26: "Throughout Kosovo, forces of the FRY and Serbia engaged in a deliberate and widespread or systematic campaign of destruction of property owned by Kosovo Albanian civilians." Paragraph 27 reads on: "In addition to the deliberate destruction of property owned by Kosovo Albanian civilians, forces of the FRY and Serbia conducted widespread and systematic acts of violence and brutality against Kosovo Albanian civilians." Again, I think still better yet, paragraph 25 illustrates what I'm saying. "Forces of the FRY and Serbia, in a deliberate and widespread or systematic manner, forcibly expelled and internally displaced hundreds of thousands of Kosovo Albanians from their homes across the entire province of Kosovo." [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So the point I respectfully submit is not that the Prosecution intends to prove with direct and specific evidence, and the Court could not make findings in respect to the non-charged incidents or sites which are referred to in the report, but the Court will deliberate on the widespread, systematic nature and the questions of the scale throughout the -- to quote the indictment "throughout Kosovo." And the report, in those circumstances, can offer some assistance in those deliberations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And are you saying that you won't be leading evidence, direct evidence, from witnesses that would be sufficient to make the finding of widespread and systematic conduct?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, I'm not saying that. In fact, with -- the -- the report would support a finding, it is the submission of the Prosecution, that the Court would be entitled to make from the evidence, the direct evidence, given by these witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Now, it has been said here that there were facsimile reports, at least two others, and this report has nothing -- as if it is not something original. But there were two other reports of the same kind, verbatim. Would you like to comment on that, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, I -- and please forgive my remission in not doing so earlier. I had intended to comment on that by submitting that -- Mr. Visnjic is indeed right. There probably were even more than two where the identical verbatim information were on different forms, allegedly or apparently submitted by different collecting agencies. If I may just reflect on the evidence first. The witness was asked questions about how this might have happened. And it is, no doubt, clear to the Court that she was put in a position where she could only speculate. She did not know how that could have happened because that would be a breach of the procedures that she sought to enforce. However, the documents that were shown to the Court were clearly print-outs from a database, and the question I asked in re-examination I think would have indicated to the Court that she would not be incognizant of nor would she know about how the material was organised, prepared, possibly merged for data-processing purposes. So that is completely out of her knowledge. So it does not, as was submitted by counsel, reflect prejudicially on her objectivity. Firstly, it -- she was asked to speculate and said she didn't know but it could have been so and so and so. The documents were received and efforts were made to put them on a database. The merger of the information in a document, apparently from the ICG and one from the OSCE, was done in an attempt to put together a usable, searchable database with all of these thousands of reports. So it does not impact on the evidence of the witness, but it is a matter which could be further explained, and I'm trying to get a precise statement as to how it happened. But it is already clear, based on the investigations that I have made, that that was something that was done here for electronic searching purposes of the various reports. But the one person still at OTP who would be able to give the details is not here this week I'm told. But if the Court requests further information, I will find out and submit it when it's available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp. Now, if I can go back to the contents of the report. Part I is historical and political background, followed by something about the human rights operation. Now, the first part of that, the historical and political background, is not a matter in which the witness claimed to have any expertise, nor did she claim to have any knowledge beyond just having been in the area at various periods over a number of years. Now, are you going to have her tell us, through this report, about Prince Lazar and the Ottoman forces and the battle of Kosovo Polje, or are now there going to be some limits on this evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: There has to be limits, it is the submission of the Prosecution, in the way that the Tribunal judges it useful in what weight can be given to and what weight cannot be given to. But in assessing the credibility of other areas of the report of more directly relevant analyses in the report, it may well be useful to the Tribunal to have -- to the Trial Chamber to have a knowledge or an appreciation of the context in which the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we'll have plenty of evidence about that, at least hopefully evidence from one reliable source. And it's the same with chapter 3, Yugoslav forces in Kosovo and the Kosovo Liberation Army. You're going to be tendering evidence through a witness you describe as an expert, Mr. Coo. Now, is that not adequate? What happens if there's any difference between the two? What do we do with it? How do we assess the reliability of this when we don't actually know who it was that compiled this paragraph, or this chapter rather?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What I am submitting, I agree that there is insufficient indicia of reliability in respect to certain areas. I think I conceded that earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Including, to some degree, the first part and the second part. But as I submitted earlier. It is a matter of context. The Court is not only interested in the context in which the offences were committed, which is what directly these parts of the report cover, but the context in which -- or the state of mind in which it was written and analysed. It is why, for example, in cross-examination one counsel for the Defence asked various questions relating to facts and statements made in various parts of the report. Because sometimes in understanding or in coming to an appropriate understanding of a particular part of the analysis in the report it might be useful to the Chamber to understand the context in which the writers of the report operated. And to that the Prosecution submits that the whole report would be useful, but some parts, obviously, would not be of sufficient probative value or reliability for it to form part of the deliberations or for a decision to be based partly or fully upon it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, if you take also paragraph -- sorry, chapter 7, rape and other forms of sexual violence, what are you going to invite us to draw from that chapter?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The -- there would be significant amount of evidence, including expert evidence, in respect to rapes being committed as part of the campaign of persecutions, as alleged. Should the Chamber accept the direct evidence of rape of these witnesses, the Prosecution would submit that that section of the book can assist the Court in its deliberations in respect to the whole issue of rape, the systematic and widespread campaign, including the offences of rape as alleged in the indictment. May I rephrase that? If I could go back to an earlier submission I made. That section would not be a section that could stand alone. The Prosecution would not be asking the Court to rely on a section like that on its own. But there will be evidence presented to the Court by individuals and by experts about rape in the course of the events that the indictment refers to. And if the Court accepts that direct evidence, it would be the submission of the Prosecution at a later stage in the proceedings that the Court could use the section of the book in -- to assist it in determining how widespread it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: On one view, that is using that type of evidence for the most significant purpose. One rape has little impact on this indictment, and if you prove two or three, that has little impact on this indictment. And that's without, for a moment, suggesting that each one of these is not a horrendous event; it is. But the thing that really matters for you is to show that it's widespread and systematic. And that's what you then invite the Trial Chamber to conclude from this material, I suspect, in relation to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- rape. It may be different in relation to some of the other crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. But if I could put it this way, we would invite the Court to use this material in support of other material. We would not ask the Court to make that type of conclusion from this type of material alone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I follow that, but you're still using it to, in that context, provide the bulk of your evidence, I suspect, the weightiest part of your evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I would submit not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There's just one final matter I want to raise with you. This is not one report but two, and the second one covers a period from June to October 1999, which is beyond the indictment. What is the purpose of this report, or part of the report?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The exhibit being tendered --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is it only the one --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- in e-court is part I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Only part I?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Although there is some relevant evidence in respect of part II that we hope might assist the Court in the deliberations on the integrity and objectivity of the witness and the procedure, because part II, as she testified, was her investigations of offences committed against the Serbs by the KLA and the Kosovar Albanians after the NATO intervention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, who is your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Goran Stoparic, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you'll have the witness ready for us when we return after the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think he's been waiting for a long time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, do you have any desire at all to hear any further comments from the Defence in this matter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: For example, in relation to what?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: In relation to the admissibility of this report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no. But give me an example of a point that you feel --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Well, yes, Mr. Stamp says that they don't intend to introduce this report as direct evidence of the crime scenes, but they do intend to use it to assist the Trial Chamber on the issue of notice to the higher-level political and military figures of crimes committed not only in 1998 but also in 1999. That really concerns the Defence in this case. That's a pivotal issue in this case, because even getting by the crime scenes, the question is: Can any one of these six defendants be proven beyond a reasonable doubt to have been part of a plan to create these crime scenes, to instigate them, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the report certainly can't achieve that because it's not produced until after the events are all over. But if the suggestion is being made that the evidence in there somehow or other supports the notion that the accused are on notice, it certainly couldn't do so on its own. He's not at any stage suggested that this material would establish that on its own. But I accept what you say, the submission was that it would assist the Trial Chamber in determining the question of notice. We have to evaluate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes. And our comment, Your Honour, is that there -- the OSCE is almost being presented to the Court as an amicus curiae. I think they have no right to be an amicus curiae in this case. It's up to the parties, I submit, Your Honour, I respectfully submit, to offer the guidance that's needed by the Court in determining the ultimate issues in this case, not the OSCE.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The various submissions made will be considered. We will not give an instant answer to this. I did say that we would try to give a fairly quick response; however, whether that's a final answer remains to be seen. There will be a fairly quick response, but it may not finally determine the issue. That I can't say for sure until we've had a chance to discuss it privately. We will adjourn now and we will resume at 4.15.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May it please Your Honour. Before we proceed with the witness, I don't know if this would be a convenient time for me to put on the record that the exhibits that we would be wished to be received in respect of the evidence by Sandra Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there any doubt about --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, there might be an issue. We thought it would be placed if it was placed on the record because in her statement some of them are referred to ERN numbers and although she does give the descriptions and the dates, but we would prefer to put the P numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: First is P432, that is the agreement on the organisation for security and cooperation in Europe, Kosovo Verification Mission, signed by the chairman of the OSCE and the FRY minister of foreign affairs dated the 19th of October, 1998; the next is P456, that is the UN Security Council Resolution 1199, adopted on the 23rd of September, 1998; P473, As Seen, As Told; P615, that is a Kosovo atlas. We do agree with the -- with you, Your Honour, that perhaps it is a little bit untidy, but it does contain some material which is not in the other atlas, and we could in due course submit upon it some more, but we ask if it is not received it could be at least marked for identity. P761, that is the OSCE Kosovo Verification Mission human rights task overview for November/December 1998; P763, that's the OSCE-KVM mission standard operating procedure, allegations of serious violations of humanitarian law of November 1999; P763 that's the OSCE-KVM human rights division operational plan of 17th of December, 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've given us that number twice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, you've just given us it and now you're giving us it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. The next is P764, the OSCE-KVM refugee monitoring plan. Then P765, the form that was disclosed. That is the OSCE-KVM refugee monitoring form. And finally P766, the OSCE-KVM verification mission -- OSCE-KVM guidelines on classifications. That is it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And for the avoidance of doubt, P473 is simply part I?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Part I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Stoparic, if you would stand, please. And I invite you to make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Stoparic, I'd like just to explain to you a little about what's going to happen here. You're about to be asked questions by a number of people, starting with the Prosecutor, who's on his feet to your right. And he will be followed by others on behalf of the accused. What you're being asked to do is answer the questions which are asked of you. This isn't a situation where you're here simply to give an account as you choose to give an account, but you're invited to confine your comments to answers to the specific questions which are given. Now, you may find that it's a nice easy time you have or you may find that some counsel ask you difficult questions and perhaps even make suggestions to you about the way in which you're answering questions. I want to make it clear to you from the outset that that's the form of procedure under which this trial is conducted. It may be one different from that in your own country or any other procedure that you yourself are familiar with. But it's important in the interests of everyone, and particularly in the interests of the accused here, that what you do is concentrate very closely on the question that's asked you and answer the question, the specific question that is put you. Thank you very much. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Mr. Stoparic, would you state your name for the record and spell your last name, please.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: My name is Goran Stoparic, S-t-o-p-a-r-i-c.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the first thing I'd like to do is have you shown a copy of your statement, Exhibit P2224, the B/C/S version for you and English for the rest of us, please. Will you let me know when you see that on the screen.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recognise what that is?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: This is the front page of what is probably my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can we scroll down so we can see the bottom of that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you recall giving a statement on the 6th of July here at the OTP?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. And you had a chance to review that at the time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you were able to read it and have it read to you before you signed it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was able to read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And are you ready to confirm now under oath that that's your true and accurate statement to the best of your knowledge and belief?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Sir, I can confirm that I see the front page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Would you like to see the rest of the pages one at a time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: You're asking me to confirm whether this is indeed my statement. I can tell you that this is certainly its front page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can we show him the next page, please. As a matter of fact, Your Honour, it may be easier if we hand him a hard copy that we have here, which I can confirm to the Court is the same as what's in the electronic copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, please do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, the -- I was expecting that if this was a witness giving evidence under Rule -- or part of the evidence under 89(F) that we would have been provided with a copy of his statement. And you've indicated that this is a recent statement, the 6th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour. It's a compilation of three earlier statements from 2003, 2004, and 2005.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, there's an order about --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's my understanding, Your Honour, it was sent to your principal Legal Officer by e-mail on the 6th of July, 6th or 7th of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, as early as -- as recently as this afternoon I was looking for it but I still haven't received it. I mean, the order was to provide hard copy, wasn't it, of these statements or -- in e-mail is fine, but it was to produce copies directly to the Chamber, not simply to upload them into the electronic disclosure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that may have been sent to you before we had the order in hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We certainly can provide you hard copies in short order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you have copies there it would be helpful because we haven't seen them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We have one, Your Honour. We can have some additional ones made and brought to you in short order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please carry on with the checking of the statement, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And if the usher could assist me by handing the English version to Mr. Stoparic as well. To the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Stoparic, would you take a look at that and tell us if you recognise our signature or your initials on the bottom of each of those pages.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now that you've had a chance to see both of those, are you comfortable in confirming for the Court that that is your true statement?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would like to tender his statement at this time. I have a second English copy we could provide to you from the one that's in front of him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Stoparic, I want to tell you that you do have a copy of your B/C/S statement there on your table and I may from time to time ask you to refer to a specific paragraph. But if at any time you're referring to it, would you please let us all know. We want you to testify from your memory and not from what's written down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, with your permission, I'd like to lead briefly the defendant [sic] on some background material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, please do that in general where it's background, and I'll leave it to counsel to draw our attention to any concerns they have about the way in which you're proceeding.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, I want to ask you a brief series of questions. If you'll wait until I finish and let me know if what I've just said is correct. You were born in 1968 in the town of Sid in Serbia. You completed your high school in 1986. You joined the JNA for your one year of military service in 1987 where you specialised in infantry reconnaissance and you served in Pristina. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Except for the place of birth. I was born in Sremska Mitrovica and I live in Sid.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And after your service in the army in 1987, you worked with your father in construction until 1991?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And we see in your statement that in July 1991 you volunteered at your local office of Territorial Defence. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: To be more precise, at the office of the Territorial Defence of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In paragraph 5 of your statement you say: "I fell for this nationalistic ideology as thousands of other Serbs did ..." What nationalistic ideology are you talking about there?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, if a young man feels the need to engage in a war against the other party, which in this case were Croats, of course it had a nationalist aspect to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And from whom or where were you hearing this nationalistic ideology?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: From all sides. From the media, from the conversations with the people at large.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: After you volunteered with the TO, you shortly had an opportunity to join a different unit. What unit was that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Following war operations in Slavonia and Baranja and Vukovar, is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, you first volunteered for the Territorial Defence. Did you actually join them and work with them?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's all right. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: After that we were joined with the 1st Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was that a unit of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That was a JNA unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how long did you stay with them?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Until the fall of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall when that was, approximately?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I couldn't give you the date. In November of 1991 -- I'm not sure. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And after that did you leave the JNA to join another group?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes. After that I went home.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: To Sid?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what happened there?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: In Sid, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. Did you join another unit?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes. Later on I joined the Skorpions unit at Djeletovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who or what were the Skorpions?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: What I knew of them at the time -- well, I joined the Skorpions upon the invitation of their commander. What I knew of the Skorpions at the time was that they were stationed in the village of Djeletovci, that one of their missions at the time was to monitor the borders or the area within their responsibility and to guard the Krajina Oil Company facilities, which was already in existence at the time, I believe, although I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who was the commander who invited you to join?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Slobodan Medic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know him by a nickname as well?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes, we all called him Boca.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, what kind of organisation or group was the Skorpions? Was it a military unit? A social unit? An army unit? If you know.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: The Skorpions consisted of two companies, one reconnaissance platoon and a working platoon. They were very well equipped in terms of infantry, weapons, in terms of uniforms, all-terrain vehicles, and so on. Of course it was a military unit. I'm not sure I fully understand your question. A military unit?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, that's my question. You mentioned uniforms. What kind of uniforms did the Skorpions have?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: They weren't always the same. As far as I know, they always had better uniforms than the Serb army. It was more up-to-date, more modern.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And were the Skorpions a part of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who did they belong to, if anyone?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: From what I know, officially they were supposed to be part of the Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. I also know that a lot of influence over the unit was wielded from the MUP of Serbia, although I don't know how this came about or how it was materialised.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You used the term "officially" when you referred to them belonging to the Army of Republic of Serbia [sic]. Was there some unofficial membership in some other group?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honours, just if we can pause for a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There is a mistake in the transcript. The witness didn't say that they belonged to the Army of the Republic of Serbia but to the Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. I think the interpretation was accurate; it's the transcript that's inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's what I heard, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, let me ask that question again. You said officially they belonged to the Army of the Republika Srpska Krajina. Was there some unofficial membership in some other group?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
