utterances.text: Some other group. To my knowledge when we had meetings when the commander and when he gave us assignments and from conversations with other members of the unit, they always said that it was the Serb state security that was behind that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And there's an abbreviation for the Serb state security that you use in your statement?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: It wasn't used by me only, it was used by everyone, and it was the DB.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In your statement in paragraph 10 you mention the Red Berets as being the skeleton of all DB special units. You mention the Skorpions as being a satellite. Were you aware of other satellite units?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: According to the stories at the time and based on what I know now, those were Arkan's Tigers, too, and there were some other units in the Republika Srpska, yes, in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In paragraph 16 of your statement, which I believe is on page 4 of your B/C/S, I want to quote. You say: "The order came from the top that 60 per cent of our men should be from the RS and RSK and 40 per cent from Serbia." And you go on to say that: "... that was so people at the top in Serbia could always deny the link between the Skorpions and Serbia." First of all, in that statement where you're talking about the RS and the RSK, are you referring to Republika Srpska and the Republika Srpska Krajina?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who told you about this order from the top?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Once I asked Srdjan Manojlovic, who was person number two in the Skorpions. He was the one distributing salaries and issuing us with equipment. He was, I believe, formerly a JNA officer, a commissioned or a non-commissioned officer. At any rate he was part of the Skorpions. On one occasion I asked him about two or three friends of mine who wanted to join the Skorpions, and he told me precisely what is written here, that there was an order coming from the top that whoever joined the unit from Serbia should stay, but that they should no longer receive people from Serbia, only from Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And based on what he told you, what was your understanding about who the top was that the order came from? Was that a particular individual or a particular organisation?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes. When one referred to the top at the time, to me it meant Belgrade, certainly not Beli Manastir or any other town. That was my understanding of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And any particular person or organ in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Throughout the time there was stories going around in the unit, and some platoon commanders used to say that we were there under the control of the DB -- well -- but I wouldn't be able to go into that. I can only tell you what Manojlovic told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, do you have English copies now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And it may be that, Mr. Hannis, we should get -- move forward into 1998 and 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm coming there shortly, Your Honour. I think in three more questions I'll be to 1995 and then I'll be to 1999 in three more questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In paragraph 17 you mentioned that certain persons that Boca, Slobodan Medic, reported to. Could you give us their full names. You mention Legija, Mrgud, Frenki, and Stanisic. If you know, can you tell us the full names of those individuals?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Legija appears to be the first one here and his name was Milorad Dulovic, and I know Boca reported to him when we were in the field in Velika Kladusa. The next person is Mrgud, and I don't know what his name was. All I know is that he became quite a popular person when he signed an agreement. Then there's Frenki whose last name is Simatovic, and Stanisic whose first name is Jovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know what position Mrgud held, even though you don't know his name?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I forgot his name, but I may be able to recall it at a later stage. He was one of the ministers within the government of the Krajina. I don't know whether he was in charge of defence or perhaps he was in some other ministry. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, between late 1991 and 1995, when you joined the Skorpions, did you, as a member of the Skorpions, take part in any combat or military operations in Croatia or Bosnia? Just yes or no, first of all.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: First you said Croatia. Our standing base was in Djeletovci, and we were tasked to be there. There were no military operations, apart from occasional reconnaissance and laying out mines as well as securing the area that was within our responsibility. As regards Bosnia, yes, we went out in Bosnia. We were in the field in the Bihac theatre, as well as in Velika Kladusa. I believe in Velika Kladusa we were headquartered in the village of Podzuvic [phoen] and we went out to a part called Treskavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. You tell us in your statement that you left the Skorpions in 1995 and opened a cafe bar in your hometown of Sid. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: With my then-girlfriend, yes. Not in 1995, though, a bit later.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to move forward then to paragraph 31 of your statement. You mentioned that several former Skorpions and MUP police hung out at your cafe bar, and you say: "Situation in Kosovo was a main topic of conversation." In late 1998 and early 1999, can you tell us what was being said by those former Skorpions and MUP police about the situation in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I don't know what was being said by the Skorpions because they were not in existence then. They were disbanded after the signing of the Erdut agreement. The policemen who returned from Kosovo mentioned of the increase of terrorist attacks of the then-UCK, or the Kosovo Liberation Army, as well as their terrorist organisation and that the situation was a grave one, although it was never officially stated. But there was an expectation that NATO would eventually be deployed, and it did at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In paragraph 32 you mention that you noticed a number of the MUP officers returning from tours of duty in Kosovo had large amounts of money and jewellery. You say it was obvious to you that that was the proceeds of looting. Can you tell the Court why you came to that conclusion. What did you know about them or what was going on that led you to think that that was the case?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Did you say "many" or "several" officers? I didn't quite understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You said you saw MUP officers returning, and it -- you said it was obvious to you that the money and jewellery -- you didn't say a number.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes. I know of some cases. This was probably my answer to someone's question. Nevertheless, it is absolutely true. Some people boasted that they simply took those things from there. As regards money, I believe that the people in the field did receive increased salaries as well, but there was always the possibility of someone appropriating something.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In paragraph 5 [sic] you mention that Boca was reforming the Skorpions. And he told you that if you were to re-enlist or join up again, this time you would be attached to the SAJ of the MUP. Do you know what SAJ was, and can you explain that to the Judges?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Up until then, until that visit by Boca, when he came to my house to invite me to accompany him to Kosovo, I knew very little. I know that his headquarters were in Batajnica and that they were an elite unit, being the best special forces that Serbia had. And for me it was an honour to fight next to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you know what kind of unit it was and to whom -- to which organ or agency it belonged?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: What I do know is that they were an anti-terrorist unit of the Serbian MUP that was in charge of public security.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Are you aware of -- well, can you tell us what MUP is. I don't know if we've talked about that before now. What was the MUP in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: The Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the SAJ was on the public security side of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were you familiar with another group called the PJP?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: This is the abbreviation for the special or separate police units.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who did they belong to?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: To the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What was the difference between the PJP and the SAJ, if you know?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: As I said, the SAJ was a special anti-terrorist unit of the Serbian MUP founded in the 1980s, as far as I know. It was the MUP's elite unit. The PJP is the following. From every OUP, meaning from every police station in Serbia, there were people taken who were well-trained and strong and they were assigned to the OUP. They had their regular duties to carry out, but in addition they attended special training and they were members of the PJP, which would then be activated under extraordinary circumstances. In any case, these were police officers of the public security sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So if I understand correctly, then PJP were regular policemen who had been sent for specialised training?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: They were regular policemen and they had some special training, perhaps a bit more extensive one than they would have otherwise received in their hometowns.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And after they got their special training to be PJP policemen, where did they go? Did they get a different assignment? Did they go back to their home police stations? How did that work?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Sir, I was never an active police officer; therefore, I can only offer my opinion. As far as I know, they were always employed with their home unit, being the OUP. But in extraordinary circumstances, there was a need for the state to take strong young people from those regular units and to put them together, to intervene wherever it was needed. It needn't be in Kosovo and Metohija itself, but anywhere in the state or even in their respective hometowns.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I'm trying to understand the difference between PJP and SAJ. I know you said SAJ was a special anti-terrorist unit. These were, as I understand, also policemen who had gotten some special training. What happened with them after they got their special training to be in SAJ? Did they go back to the police stations or did they have some kind of separate posting?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: What I do know of the SAJ is the following. The SAJ wouldn't take people from the civilian sector, meaning civilians. For someone to become a member of the SAJ and to undergo their training, that person must have been a police officer prior to that, or at least must have completed the police academy.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So could a civilian go straight to PJP for training?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: No. Maybe in case they carried out some training with the reserves, with the police reserves as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What about -- between the two, between SAJ and PJP, was one better equipped? Was one seen to be more special or more elite than the other, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: All police officers are well-trained. The PJP was well-equipped as well, but the SAJ is the SAJ, the chosen ones. They probably underwent much more strict and heavier training. They are a special anti-terrorist unit, as their name testifies, and they are but a few.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And there's another acronym I think that you referred to in your statement somewhere, the JSO. Can you tell us who or what they were?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: The JSO, the unit for special operations, called by many the Red Berets.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And were they also a part of the Ministry of Interior?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were they on the public security side of the Ministry of Interior?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: No. They were on the state security side.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can you tell us what the acronym or the abbreviation is for state security. You told us DB was, I think, the acronym. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes. The DB means "drzavna bezbednost," state security.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. And is there an acronym for public security?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I would have guessed so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now I'd like to move on to -- well, let me summarise a little bit and then ask you a question. In paragraphs 39 to 49, that's pages 7 through 9 of the B/C/S and pages 7 through 9 of the English, you describe how a group -- you and a group of about 120 volunteers, Skorpions, went from Sid to Kosovo. And I note in paragraph 45 of your statement, I believe on page 8, that you said about 50 per cent of the volunteers in this group had no combat experience. Do you know if they had any prior police experience?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I don't know. As far as I know, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you tell us in your statement that this group of volunteers were going to be a detachment of the SAJ, the special anti-terrorist unit, the elite unit. Based on your past experience, did you think it unusual that men with such a lack of experience would be assigned to that elite unit?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I was quite surprised by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned that you actually gave them some training in house and street fighting during the couple of days before you actually arrived in Kosovo. Did you -- during that time did you or did they receive any training or instruction about the Geneva Conventions on dealing with prisoners of war or civilians encountered in combat zones?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I didn't instruct anyone about that and I wasn't instructed by anyone, but the only training I did have concerning that was back from 1987 when I served my military term with the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, I want to go next to Kosovo. In your statement in paragraphs 50 through 64, pages 9 through 11 in both versions, you date an event in Podujevo, Kosovo, in which Sasa Cvetan and three other Skorpions shot and killed a group of 19 Albanian civilians, including 12 children under the age of 14. And then you talk about how you were all sent back to Serbia and told to take ten days' leave. You then say around the middle of April you and many of that original group that had first gone there returned to Kosovo. When you returned, was Sasa Cvetan in the group that returned?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Sasa Cvetan was not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What about the other three shooters, were they in the group that returned?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: They all returned to Kosovo, the entire unit, except for Sasa Cvetan.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were the -- were the identities of the other three involved in the shooting known to the superiors of the Skorpions at the time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were those three ever disciplined or charged that you know of?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: One man was charged. He was later acquitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know why the other two were not charged?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Someone must have obstructed the investigation, probably the commander himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to go forward to paragraph 64 through 79 of your statement. I think it's pages 11 through 13. You describe how you had returned to Kosovo in mid-April and you talk about your participation in some operations to drive out the UCK or KLA and "seized the villages and hamlets. This was called cleaning." And you say this took place in the area of Jezerce in the municipality of Suva Reka and then north of Strpce. During these operations, did you see any Kosovo Albanians? And let me first say: Did you see any Kosovo Albanian civilians?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: From a distance. I saw them in groups leaving.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you did encounter some KLA opposition?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you continued to be active in this operation until you were shot and wounded on the 2nd of May, 1999 by a KLA fire?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I understand then that you were hospitalised first in Pristina, then to the Belgrade Military Academy, where you had some operations on your arm and your elbow, and that wound left you permanently medically unfit for military purposes?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in May of 2000 you got an award for your work as a member of the SAJ of the MUP of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I don't see that as an award. I had been wounded and I received a special commendation for my exceptional work on combatting terrorism in the area of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who was that from?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Vlajko Stojiljkovic signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And he was the minister of the interior of Serbia at the time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were the Serbians who were the volunteers with you when you came back to Kosovo, they were the -- they were volunteers and you volunteer Skorpions were attached to the SAJ. Correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who were the Skorpions attached to when you came back to Kosovo in mid-April?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, they were attached to the reserve forces of the SAJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to go to paragraphs 83 to 87 of your statement, which are on pages 13 and 14 of the English and page 14 of the B/C/S. In those paragraphs, Mr. Stoparic, you describe the criminal proceedings or the trials against Sasa Cvetan for the 1999 killing of those civilians in Podujevo. You were called as a witness in both those proceedings. Could you tell the Judges in your own words what happened the first time you were called as a witness in that matter. Were you spoken to by anyone from the Defence before you appeared on that case?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: No. I spoke to the Defence counsel --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, you're being asked to repeat that answer, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was asked whether before testifying in those proceedings I spoke to anyone, whether I spoke to the Defence. I said not only did I speak with the Defence counsel but I was also visited by the family of the accused as well as the Skorpions commander and several of his men whom he used as body-guards. In total, around 20 people spoke to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what did those people tell you or ask you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: That we needed to defend Sasa.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Anything else? How were you going to do that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I was supposed to appear at a proceedings at Prokuplje, I believe. I met on several occasions with the Defence counsel. And on the day I was to testify together with two other witnesses, we went in one car down to the south of Serbia. Boca, the commander, ordered that we all -- all three of us come to his property. And he said: Be careful what you do there. If you spill your beans you won't live for long. And I was given a paper by the attorney with a statement or with the answers I was supposed to provide. It was rather brief, the way he authored that text. And he gave it not only to me but to the other witnesses as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So what happened when you actually went to testify in that first trial? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I was asked to say that once the shooting started and once we all headed toward the place the shooting was coming from, that Sasa was running alongside me and that the only thing he did was to fire a burst of fire some 15 minutes earlier which was only meant to serve to speed up the people as they were walking, merely that. And that was in fact my statement at that trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was that the truth?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: No, it is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how did you feel after that afterwards, knowing that you had lied about it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, of course I felt badly about it, especially in view of the fact that so many children had been killed, but still my life was at stake. It was terrible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What did you do as a result of that, as a result of feeling bad about it? Did you do anything?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Many eye-witnesses of the incidents live in my hometown and we talked about it a lot, and we all agreed that whoever killed those children deserved to be punished. However, it was dangerous for us to speak up and to voice these things at trial. First of all, one man was standing trial, and we all know that one person was unable to kill 19 persons in one minute, even if the victims were children. I don't know. I wanted to tell the truth, but I simply did not have the chance to do that before that trial in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You mentioned the first trial, and I think you said or you say in your statement that was in Prokuplje. Where is Prokuplje? Pardon my pronunciation.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: It's in the south of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you just mentioned there was a second trial in Belgrade. Do you remember when that took place?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: The second trial went on for quite a while. I know that I testified in the month of December of 1993, I believe.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Or 4. I don't know. I must have forgotten. Well, two or three years ago at any rate.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The transcript showed "1993," and since the events happened in 1999 I assume that was just a mistake.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: 2003, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. How -- did you come to be a witness in the second trial?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, the first time I was a witness for the Defence. However, when the case was referred from the court in Prokuplje to Belgrade, the prosecutor in that case called all the witnesses appearing in the first trial as prosecution witnesses, and I was among them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you -- did you tell a different version of what happened in the second trial?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: At the second trial I told the things as they happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And that was that Sasa and three others did the shooting?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: During that trial I confirmed that the Skorpions perpetrated that act and that I saw Sasa and other people coming out of that yard. I never said that I saw them shoot.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I understand. And was that the truth?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Sir, at that trial Mr. Tutinac said the same thing I did. Yes, the Skorpions fired upon those children, and that's the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What -- what caused you to change your mind? How were you able to tell the truth this time? Were you still in fear for your life?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Of course I was. Even at that trial in Belgrade when I received the summons, I entered the courtroom and told the Bench that I did not feel very well and that I should be invited some other time. And this was because before entering the courtroom I met Boca in the corridor, who again offered to give me money, vehicles, in exchange for a statement that would enable Sasa to defend himself. Furthermore, at the entrance to the court I saw two of his men who, upon seeing me, went away. And probably he, having heard that people would be invited again to testify, wanted to make sure that they told the right story. That was why I went out of the courtroom that day, but I came back to testify under police protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think in your statement you indicated that Boca had offered you a large sum of money. Do you remember how much that was?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I think he said something along the lines of 100.000, but he could have named any sum.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: 100.000 what currency?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Marks, euros, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, I assume that in addition to being afraid for your life, being offered a bribe of 100.000 Deutschmarks, what did you think was going to happen to you if you told the truth as far as your relationships with other Skorpions or former Skorpions?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Many of the Skorpions did not hold this against me; those who did were, in a way, related to these events and were afraid of being imprisoned. Of course I was afraid what would -- of what would become of me. And after my testimony at this trial, I was given police protection for another month.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in spite of that fear, you went ahead and told the truth. Why? Why did you do that? It seemed like it would have been easy to just tell the same lie.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, I was offended by him. First of all, he offered me money; second of all, he threatened me, although he did not always do it in person. I received his messages through other members of the Skorpions, and I mean threatening messages. But anyway, I had decided to tell the truth six months earlier. And I told the story at this trial. I was given police protection for that one day of testimony, but I was actually given real police protection after my testimony. I was testifying at the district court of Belgrade as well as at this special court and I was a cooperating witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You said you made the decision six months earlier to tell the truth. At that time what was the deciding factor for you to tell the truth in spite of your concerns?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I would have wished you to have eye-witnessed the killing of so many children, innocent children, and then I would be the one to ask you that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Will we break at 5.30, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think 5.45. We started at 4.15, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I just have two other things to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I think in the circumstances, perhaps we should then adjourn just now and --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I just have a couple more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we'll adjourn now, I think, Mr. Hannis, and we'll resume at ten minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The first thing I'd like to do is ask the usher to hand hard copies of two documents to the witness. And for us on e-court I'd like to bring up first P951.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, if you could look first at the thicker of those two documents. I think it has a date on it of 28 June 2005 and it's -- appears to be a matter concerning the district court in Belgrade. When you prepared your 89(F) statement for today when we met last week, did you have a chance to look at that document?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you recognise it as relating to the trial proceedings in which you've testified against Mr. Cvetan the second time in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now if we could bring up 952.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Stoparic, if you would look at the skinnier document dated 3 March 2006. Now I'll ask you the same question: Did you have a chance to look at that one as well?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And this appears to be an appeal related to that same case. That also involved the trial of Sasa Cvetan? I'm sorry. I don't know if you heard me. I asked a question. Did that involve your trial? I didn't see your answer. Does that second document involve the trial that you testified in in Belgrade against Sasa Cvetan?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'd like to tender these two at this time. And with that, I have no further questions of this witness. But before we begin cross-examination, Your Honour, I would request permission to go into private session for two minutes to address an issue concerning to -- concerning this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Private session. Mr. O'Sullivan, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I'm just wondering on the propriety of doing it -- making these submissions in the presence of the witness. If Mr. Hannis could make that determination perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't have a problem with the witness being out of the room while I address this. However, I can see a point where it may become necessary for the Court to inquire of the witness regarding it as well. So I don't know which is more efficient. Perhaps we can do it with him out of the room and maybe we can resolve it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're satisfied, Mr. O'Sullivan, that there's a risk of interfering with his evidence if he's here while we discuss this issue, are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I think Mr. Hannis can probably anticipate that. That's my only concern. If, in fact, we came to that point that would be a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I guess I'd rather err on the side of safety and have him step out of the room briefly while we discuss this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, you've heard the exchange just now. There is an issue of law to be dealt with. Could you briefly please leave the courtroom. You'll come back in a moment or two, but please leave us while we have this discussion on a matter of law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And we should now go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'll proceed in the following order. First, counsel for Lukic; Pavkovic; Milutinovic; Sainovic; Ojdanic; and Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Stoparic, you are to be cross-examined by counsel for the accused, and the first counsel to conduct that cross-examination will be Mr. Lukic, who represents the accused Mr. Lukic. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. But before I address the witness, I have to ask you for one procedural matter, and I'm sorry I didn't raise it before. Do you wish to enter the prior statements of this witness as exhibits, or you prefer me just to go through them without entering them as exhibits? And the practice in this Tribunal is different from Chamber to Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are they Prosecution exhibits in the case?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, they are not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you are presenting them as part of your library of exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure. Should I or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Have they been introduced into the e-court system as yet?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We potentially put some of them, but I'm not sure if we have English versions of all of them. But if it's not on the e-court -- we have English versions copied for Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it would be helpful if you would, in future, follow the procedure which was set out in the order, that these should be introduced into the e-court system, unless there is some reason why that can't be done, in which case you will have to seek on good cause shown relief from the Trial Chamber to allow you to make use of documents. Now, in this case I see no reason why these should not have been entered into the e-court system in accordance with that ruling. However -- and if that happens, as soon as you refer to the document and you give it its number, it will simply be a document that's part of the trial process, unless someone has objected to its admission and we've had a debate on its admissibility and then we have to take a positive decision. But in the absence of objection, any document that's part of your library of documents for the case will simply be part of the record of the case as it is used. So in this case you don't need to do anything formal. You can present these documents and see if any objection is taken when you invite the witness to look at the document and deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The only reason why we hesitated is we don't know your position on prior statements of the same witness, whether they should be an exhibit or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I -- well, are you raising this on the basis that for some reason you shouldn't disclose it in advance? Or are you raising it in a general basis is it an exhibit or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In a general basis because those are the statements given to the Prosecutor by the same witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you introduce them and they're not part of the Prosecution's library of exhibits, then they must be your exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. We have all of them already in the system, so I would like two of them to be released --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So they are in the system?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Right. Good.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The only problem again we have is that the first one -- the first statement given by this witness is from 2003, and we don't have English version in the system, but we provided printed version for Your Honours so you can follow. And as soon as we find this English version, we'll attach it to the system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. All right. Anyway, let's get started with the cross-examination, and when we come to the statements no doubt you will alert us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that we are already there, Your Honour, because I'll go through the statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, does that mean we need to go back into private session now? I'm finding this very confusing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You are not the only one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you're supposed to be in control of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't have to go to private session yet because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- I'm not at that point yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Carry on then.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And with your permission, Your Honours, I would like to conduct this cross-examination in B/C/S because it would be -- I could be in more control. Thanks a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Stoparic.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My name is Branko Lukic, and together with Dragan Ivetic and Mr. Ogrizovic, I appear for General Lukic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that they don't have copies of the documents used by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to clarify one little point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... just for a moment because I've just received a message from the interpreters that they don't have the documents that are going to be used. Now, Mr. Sabbah, do the interpreters not have access to the e-court? Well, all the documents except one are to be on e-court, as I understand it, then there shouldn't be a problem for the interpreters. So carry on, Mr. Lukic, thanks.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note that they only have access to what can be seen under the button "computer evidence" not to e-court as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Stop. Sorry. Let's get this clarified now. The next message is, Mr. Sabbah, that the interpreters don't have access to the e-court button or what can be brought up by the e-court button.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the updated information I'm given now is that that is what's intended in due course, but at the moment e-court is not, fact, available to the interpreters. And therefore, if you have hard copies of this material, then it may aid them if the hard copies are available for the ELMO. So perhaps your case manager or assistant who's there can do something about that while you start your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stoparic, let us resume your cross-examination. Firstly, I will ask you briefly a matter about your statement you gave on the 6th of July, 2006, several days ago, therefore. I'd like to know whether you gave this statement or was it compiled by the OTP investigators. Therefore, on the 6th of July, 2006, did you speak to them and they wrote down what you said, or was it simply a compilation of your previous statements?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I believe that the latter is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That they compiled your statements?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that they used two or three of my statements to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who decided what should be inserted in the statement dated the 6th of July, 2006? Was it you or was it them?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I don't understand. What do you mean? I or them? Who them?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The investigators or OTP representatives, were they the ones who decided what to select out of your previous statements, or did you tell them which paragraphs of -- from those previous statements were to be put into the 6th of July, 2006 statement?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I read the statement that I was given and I agreed to it. I referred them to some of the mistakes that were there inadvertently, which normally happens.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we therefore conclude that you read this statement and then signed it, nothing more?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: No. I also participated in giving my input in terms of matters that I disagreed with or I thought were inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In this statement it states that the interviewer was Philip Caine. Do you know what Philip Caine's role was in compiling this statement?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I don't know any Philip Caine.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who was present while you were signing the statement?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: The interpreter, maybe I know this person by sight but I don't know him by name. There were people from the Prosecution of course, several of them, as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I wanted to go through several paragraphs from your latest statement, and then we will go through your first and second statement. In the statement of the 6th of July, 2006, in paragraph 47 you described the MUP building in Podujevo, which was hit by NATO bombs. During your short stay in Podujevo, did you see or hear of any other targets being hit by NATO in Podujevo up until that time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: No, I don't remember. NATO was bombing all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In that statement of the 6th of July, 2006, in paragraph 59, you described the situation after the murder of 19 civilians in Podujevo, and you say: "Tutinac was very angry and used very harsh words with us. I was afraid he would kill us all and he said that they were going to send us back. I supposed we were being sent out of Kosovo." In paragraph 60 you state: "Half an hour later all members of the Skorpions, apart from one platoon, were on buses. They left Podujevo and went towards Prolom Banja." My question, therefore, is: Do you think that such behaviour of your superiors prevented any further massacres of civilians?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes. It is absolutely possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the same statement of the 6th of July, 2006, in paragraph P67 you mentioned the operation in Jezerce in the municipality of Suva Reka. You state: "We started operations to drive the Albanian terrorists out and seize the villages and hamlets. This was called 'cleaning' or mopping up." Could you explain to us what the units participating in that operation were actually doing during the cleaning or mopping-up operation?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: We always used to do that when we were sent out for an operation. As to what exactly they did, well, they would try to seize that area, take control of it. Of course, if they met any resistance, they were supposed to eliminate it, to eliminate the KLA terrorists.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the operation in Jezerce, did you kill any civilians?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: No, we didn't see any, apart from those we saw from a distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The term "cleaning" or "mopping-up" the way you used it in your unit when carrying out operations, does that include any murders or expelling of civilians?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Throughout the war whilst I carried arms, mopping-up for me meant attacking the enemy forces [as interpreted], trying to seize control of their territory or facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement you mention --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just one correction for the transcript. In the transcript on the page 78, line 20, it is written "enemy forces," and I think that the witness mentioned "enemy soldiers."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your statement you often referred to Tutinac. Do you know what his first name was?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I even spoke on the phone with him once, but I don't know what it is. I believe I was told once what his first name was, but for me he always remained Tuta or Tutinac. I appreciate him greatly, a good professional.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could his last name be Simovic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: That is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the statement of the 6th of July, 2006, in paragraph 79, you state that you spent a total of around 15 to 16 days in Kosovo as part of the SAJ. Therefore, you were a remember of the reserve forces of the police. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I've been saying throughout.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As a reserve member of the police, do you know that you could have been attached to any reserve police unit?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I don't know that, but I wouldn't be surprised if that were a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the statement of the 24th of February, 2004, in paragraph 53 you state that you were never ordered to kill civilians. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Absolutely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would like the usher to deliver the statement to the witness as well, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stoparic, I believe you have before you the statement dated the 21st November 2003. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: It says Belgrade, the 21st, the 22nd, and the 24th.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What I meant was that the first one is the 21st of November.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 10 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think this document should probably now have a number. This must have a number in e-court, does it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Its number is 6D7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But only in Serbian, in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stoparic, in the statement of the 21st of November, 2003, in the Serbian version in paragraph 10, which is continued on page 4 of 30 you state in the second line: "I never hurt [realtime transcript read in error "heard"] anyone. I saw (redacted) killing civilians." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Is what correct, what you've just read out?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you report that to anyone?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My learned friends have some objections, so if you bear with me, Your Honour, just to consult for a second. Sorry, now I understand finally. In the transcript it says "I never heard," and should be "I never hurt anybody."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Or harm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 12 of the same statement it reads: "I saw many dead bodies of Croatian civilians in the streets of Tovarnik. I also saw the dead body of the grandmother of a friend of mine from Sid who was a Serb lady. She was probably killed when she tried to protect some Croats." Mr. Stoparic, do you know of this or is this a speculation on your part?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Is this what you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I said here of a friend of mine from Sid, and this is what he told me about what he thought had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But you don't know it for a fact, the way it really happened?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: No, of course I don't. All I saw was her dead body.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us move on to paragraph 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On B/C/S version it's page 6, but as since we don't have the English version I don't know the English page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's on --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Page 5 in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Page 5, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stoparic, in paragraph 21 you state: "We were told by Chetnik Captain Ljuba Ivanovic during the training that we had to make up for the 700.000 Serbs killed during World War II, meaning that we had to kill the same number of Croats." Did you consent to such conditions?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But you remained in the unit?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, sir, not for long. And this Chetnik captain Ljuba Ivanovic, well, he met his sudden end by the same method he employed in his actions. He was a Chetnik captain -- at least that's what he called himself. I attended his funeral in Nis, and there was a letter from the Serbian Radical Party read out there by Seselj. He thanked the Chetnik captain for his fierce fighting in the liberation of the Serb territories. As for what I stated here, that is precisely what the man said.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But you never accepted such preconditions?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I didn't kill any civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did other members of the unit accept such conditions?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: That unit was soon -- well, throughout their so-called military war career, I didn't follow what they were doing. But I saw some of those people later, and they never told me they had -- they felt any urge to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 25, there you state you were the commander of the 1st Platoon of the 1st Company.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I think I commanded the 2nd Platoon of the 1st Company.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In any case, you commanded a platoon?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us move on to paragraph 30. That is page 9 in the B/C/S and page 7 in the English. The last sentence reads: "Members of the Leva Supoderica unit often killed Croatian civilians." First of all, can you tell me what Leva Supoderica is?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Leva Supoderica is a settlement, a part of Vukovar, and that detachment was called Leva Supoderica. I presume because they hailed from that part of town, including their commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you a member of this unit?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was a member of the Leva Supoderica unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry to intervene, Your Honour, but I realise now that we've gone into the 2004 statement, and I don't think we've mentioned the exhibit number for this one. We had referred to the exhibit number for the 2003 statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it's this one that is 6D7, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I'm sorry. Then we didn't mention a number for the other one when we spoke briefly about the 2003 statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's -- I think that's correct, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Lukic, do you have a number for the 2003 statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I hope that I'm still on the same statement from the 21st November 2003, and on paragraph 3-0, 30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, yeah. Mr. Hannis, the statement we're on is 21st -- it's actually signed 24th November, 2003.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I stand corrected on that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And that seems to be the only one we've explored.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, we established that members of your unit again killed civilians. Did you take part in the killings of those civilians?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: No. Can I offer an explanation? Based on the experience I have, in every unit -- or rather, not really in every unit, not in highly professional ones, but in the units composed of volunteers where killing of civilians occurred, it was always committed by one group of people who repeatedly go back to the front line. But you can't say that where a person was a member of a unit that he automatically did what other members of the unit did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, and I accept your explanation. However, we said that you were a platoon commander. What did you do to sanction the people who were killing?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I will tell you, and I speak for my platoon. These were members of the Leva Supoderica platoon and there were many of them. There was only one case where a man reported to me and said: Oh gosh, you have to know what we were doing yesterday. I can't really quote his words, but at any rate he told me that he had killed some people, that he had run them through with a knife. I believe that it was the Ovcara people. I told him: Oh, get away, you must be lying. However, when the Ovcara trial in Belgrade commenced, this same person was convicted of that crime. You see, I've told you, I simply didn't believe him at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you ever report what you knew of the killing of civilians in Vukovar to anyone?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, who was I supposed to report that to? If these dead civilians were at the same time seen by my superior, my commander, then who was I supposed to turn to?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I wish to move on to paragraph 41 of the same statement. There you speak of Vojislav Seselj and say that the effect he left on the volunteers was that of a drug, it was intoxicating. I don't wish to dwell on Mr. Seselj now, but I'd like to ask you the following. Do you have first-hand experience with drugs and their effects on people?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Not personally, but I was able to see the effects on other people, and I learned quite a lot from books, as other people did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I wish to move to paragraph 65 of the same statement, which is on page --

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. It's page 13 in the English version. In this paragraph you state: "I had had enough of Brcko and I was unhappy with the behaviour of some members of my unit. One of my soldiers killed a married Muslim couple in a beastly way in order to rob them. I helped the police arrest the soldier." Can you tell us the name of the soldier? We can move into private session if you want.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to remember his name at this time, but for many reasons I prefer to tell his name in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, may we go into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. We shall go into private session because of the nature of the evidence which the witness is being asked to give which he says he will be unhappy to give if the evidence is heard in public.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stoparic, I'd now like you to focus on paragraph 66 of the statement. You state: "When I demobilised at Brcko sometime in the spring of 1993, I took a few of the soldiers who shared my beliefs or similar to mine and we went to Teslic to work with the HVO on a joint operation against Muslims." What were these beliefs that you shared with these soldiers?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Beliefs. Well, perhaps I didn't put it properly here, but at any rate I'll explain what I meant when I said that we shared the same beliefs. I meant to say that a soldier is a soldier and has to kill another soldier. Imagine if we took the late Ljuba Ivanovic to Zepce with HVO. Do you understand what I'm saying? We need to have a strictly professional relation. If we are ordered to do something, we have to execute that. And I know that. I was there. That's why I decided to select a few people for whom I knew that they would not cause any incidents, and that was what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you in Teslic when Micas -- the Micas operated over there?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I never heard that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, that's a legitimate answer. Thank you. I've asked you about these beliefs precisely because I wanted to ask you the following: Were these the same people who fought Croats with you in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, you are being asked to repeat that answer, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The answer was: Most of them were, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could we move to paragraph 69 on page 18. In this paragraph you speak of the inception of the Skorpions and you say: "I learned that the Skorpions were a special unit of the state security, formed as a satellite unit of the Red Berets at a meeting in Novi Sad between Mihalj Kertes, Dule Filipovic, Slobodan Grahovac, Radovan Stojicic, Badza, and Bozovic in Novi Sad. Perhaps some other people were present too. This meeting was held approximately three months before I joined the Skorpions." In what way did you learn of this meeting?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I was invited to join the Skorpions by Medic, who was accompanied by accompanied by his body-guards, or at least persons who were his body-guards at the time, and many of them were his relatives. I wanted to know more about the units and he told me: Well, I think you should steer clear of Seselj's units or any other units of that sort. You should really join units that are more professional. If you want to fight, then at least fight with someone who's more professional. He wanted to present himself as a connoisseur of all these people. There was one other name that he mentioned to me and I omitted to say. That name I think -- he also mentioned Zivko Sokolovacki who was a manager at the time or something along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So Medic told you about the meeting?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely as I said it here. And now I added Zivko Sokolovacki. I learned it from him and the people who were sitting there with him. Then I inquired after that. I wanted to know what sort of equipment they had because I wanted to make sure that I was moving on to a better post. I had had enough of these volunteer-type of units that didn't even have uniforms, and I found the story as he put it to me quite attractive. I thought it a certain post, one that was offered by the state, and I said: Well, why not?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So the only source of information in that regard was Medic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you receive other information concerning the Skorpions only from him?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I had received all my orders from him, and everything that I had to know, formally or informally, I learned from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Paragraph 70 of the same statement. At the same time, paragraph 10 in the 6th of July, 2006 statement you state that one of the satellite units was the CSB from Doboj. Do you know what the CSB is?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Based on what I heard, the CSB is the Central Security Service or something of the sort. I know that they said that Mladen Kuzemka [phoen] was the commander of the CSB. That's all I know, and the whole paragraph contains the information that was told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you want to say that the CSB Doboj was a satellite auxiliary unit?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: No, probably only their special platoon or special company.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: One part of the CSB therefore?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Please, I apologise if I made a mistake somewhere in these acronyms. Whenever I heard over the communications lines "CSB" or words to that effect, I thought that they referred to their specialists. I know that generally speaking in police terms the CSB is something larger.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 73 on page 19, that's page 14 in the English version. You state: "The state security of the RSK did not exist. There was only the state security of Serbia." You're speaking of the structure of the MUP in the Republic of the Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Which paragraph is that, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 73, that's the third line of paragraph 73. "There was no state security of the RSK."

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that for a fact or as a rumour?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I wasn't a responsible duty holder there. You could say that I heard that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Therefore, you were never in the head office of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina and you can't, therefore, claim that the ministry lacked one of its sectors entirely?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I am absolutely clear about the fact that this is contained in my statement. I did state that, but the context was different. What one needs to add here is not an opinion of mine, but simply that this was the sort of information that I received.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, I'm quite clear about that. I simply want to establish with you that you do not have any direct knowledge of this but that you're simply conveying what you heard.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: May I explain this a bit further?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: You see, sir, if something is said 100 times, even it is an untruth, it will become the truth. To me, as an ordinary person, a soldier, I simply had to grasp pieces of information and make conclusions on the basis of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is precisely what we are afraid of in testimonies when persons convey things that they are not certain of, and that's why we appreciate you saying that clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Lukic, would this be a suitable time to interrupt?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Any moment is suitable for the break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, Mr. Stoparic, we have to end the proceedings for the day at this time, and they will continue tomorrow. You should be here ready to commence your evidence at 2.15 tomorrow. Meanwhile, it is absolutely vital that you have no communication about your evidence, either that you've given or are about to give, with any person. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I understand that fully. After all, this is public testimony. I don't have to tell anyone that I will be testifying tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But the point I'm making is that you shouldn't be discussing it in any form whatsoever with any other person overnight. So please return here tomorrow, ready to begin your evidence, at 2.15. The Court is now adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 13th day of July, 2006, at 2.15 p.m. 23 24

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.00 p.m.,
